title: House Robber III
notes:
Task: Maximize the sum of selected tree-node values without selecting a node and its direct child.
Idea: Recursively return two values per subtree: best when taking its root and best when skipping it.
Invariant: Taking a node forces both children to be skipped; skipping it allows either state for each child.
Edge cases: A null node contributes zero in both states; negative values are naturally avoided when skipping is better.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once and recursion depth follows tree height.

title: House Robber III
notes:
Task: Choose tree nodes for maximum total value while never taking both a parent and its child.
Idea: Return a pair for each subtree containing the best take-root and skip-root totals.
Invariant: The take state uses children’s skip states; the skip state takes the best of each child's two states.
Edge cases: A null subtree returns two zeros; TreeNode is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Every node is processed once with recursion stack proportional to height.

title: Counting Bits
notes:
Task: Return the set-bit count for every integer from zero through n.
Idea: Reuse the answer for i shifted right one bit and add the least significant bit.
Invariant: dp[i] equals the number of set bits in the binary representation of i.
Edge cases: dp[0] is zero; the recurrence handles odd and even values without special cases.
complexity_reason: Each integer is processed once and its answer is stored in the output array.

title: Counting Bits
notes:
Task: Count one bits for all values in the range [0,n].
Idea: Compute bits[i] as bits[i/2] plus i's least significant bit.
Invariant: The value for i/2 is already available because it is smaller than i.
Edge cases: n=0 returns the one-element array [0].
complexity_reason: The loop fills n entries and the result array stores n+1 counts.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
notes:
Task: Expose nested integers as a flat iterator in left-to-right order.
Idea: Keep a stack of NestedInteger values; expand a list at the top until the top is an integer.
Invariant: The stack stores the unconsumed sequence in reverse order, with the next output at its top.
Edge cases: Empty nested lists are discarded during hasNext; NestedInteger is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Each nested item is pushed and popped once; the stack holds unconsumed items and nesting depth.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
notes:
Task: Implement next/hasNext over nested lists while preserving integer order.
Idea: Use a deque as a stack and expand the front nested list until an integer is at the front.
Invariant: The deque front is always the next unconsumed nested item in traversal order.
Edge cases: Empty inner lists are removed during hasNext; NestedInteger is supplied by the judge.
complexity_reason: Every nested item is expanded or returned once; the deque stores pending values.

title: Power of Four
notes:
Task: Determine whether n is a positive power of four.
Idea: Require a positive value with one set bit, then require that bit to be in an even position.
Invariant: n&(n-1)==0 detects a single set bit, and the mask 0x55555555 selects even bit positions.
Edge cases: Zero and negative values fail the positivity check; powers of two that are not powers of four fail the position mask.
complexity_reason: A fixed number of integer bit operations are used.

title: Power of Four
notes:
Task: Check whether an integer equals 4 raised to a nonnegative integer power.
Idea: Verify one set bit and ensure it occupies an even-numbered bit position.
Invariant: The first bit test rejects values with multiple set bits; the mask rejects odd-position powers of two.
Edge cases: n=1 is true, while n=0, negatives, and 8 are false.
complexity_reason: The method performs a constant number of bitwise operations.

title: Integer Break
notes:
Task: Split n into at least two positive integers to maximize their product.
Idea: Handle n<=3 directly, then multiply by threes while the remainder exceeds four.
Invariant: Replacing a factor of four with 2+2 is no worse than keeping 3+1, so the final remainder is at least two.
Edge cases: n=2 returns 1 and n=3 returns 2 because at least two parts are required.
complexity_reason: The loop subtracts three from n each iteration and stores only a product and remainder.

title: Integer Break
notes:
Task: Maximize the product of at least two positive integers summing to n.
Idea: Use factors of three, except leave a remainder of two, three, or four for the final factor.
Invariant: For larger n, splitting a factor into threes improves the product until the remainder is at most four.
Edge cases: n=2 returns 1; n=3 returns 2 under the required two-part split.
complexity_reason: The loop decreases n by three per iteration and uses constant storage.

title: Reverse String
notes:
Task: Reverse the character array in place without allocating another array.
Idea: Swap characters at the two ends and move both pointers inward until they meet.
Invariant: The outer positions already processed contain the corresponding reversed characters.
Edge cases: Empty and one-character arrays require no swaps; the method mutates the supplied list and returns None.
complexity_reason: Each pair is swapped once using two indices and no extra array.

title: Reverse String
notes:
Task: Reverse a character array in place using constant extra memory.
Idea: Swap symmetric characters while left is less than right.
Invariant: The processed prefix and suffix match the reversed input at their corresponding positions.
Edge cases: Odd-length inputs leave the middle character unchanged; empty arrays are valid.
complexity_reason: The loop makes at most n/2 swaps and uses one temporary character.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
notes:
Task: Reverse only vowels while keeping every consonant and its position unchanged.
Idea: Move pointers inward until each points to a vowel, then swap those two characters.
Invariant: Characters outside the active interval are already in their final positions.
Edge cases: Case-insensitive vowels are recognized; strings with fewer than two vowels need no swap.
complexity_reason: The pointers scan the string once and a character list stores the mutable copy.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
notes:
Task: Reverse the vowel order in a string without changing non-vowel positions.
Idea: Convert to a character array and swap vowels found by two inward-moving pointers.
Invariant: The prefix and suffix outside the pointers are already finalized.
Edge cases: Both lowercase and uppercase vowels count; no vowels leaves the string unchanged.
complexity_reason: Each pointer advances monotonically and the character array is linear in string length.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
notes:
Task: Return k values with the highest frequencies.
Idea: Count values, place each value in a bucket indexed by its frequency, then collect from high frequencies downward.
Invariant: Every value appears in the bucket matching its exact count.
Edge cases: Values tied at a frequency may be returned in any order; k does not exceed the number of distinct values.
complexity_reason: Counting and bucket insertion are linear, and the buckets contain at most n entries.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
notes:
Task: Select k distinct integers with greatest occurrence counts.
Idea: Count frequencies and use an array of buckets indexed by count, scanning from largest count downward.
Invariant: Each value is stored exactly once in the bucket for its frequency.
Edge cases: Equal-frequency ordering is unspecified; the method stops as soon as k values are collected.
complexity_reason: Hash counting, bucket placement, and bucket scanning each take linear time.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
notes:
Task: Return distinct values shared by two arrays.
Idea: Convert each input to a set and intersect them.
Invariant: The result contains only values present in both unique-value collections.
Edge cases: Duplicate occurrences are removed; result order is not specified.
complexity_reason: Building the two hash sets and their intersection is expected linear work.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
notes:
Task: Return each integer that occurs in both arrays, without duplicates.
Idea: Build a set from the first array and add matching values from the second to a result set.
Invariant: Every result value has appeared in both arrays and is stored once.
Edge cases: Repeated values do not duplicate output; output ordering is unspecified.
complexity_reason: Hash-set construction and membership checks take expected linear time.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
notes:
Task: Return common values with multiplicity equal to the minimum count in either input.
Idea: Count the first array and consume one count whenever a value from the second array matches.
Invariant: Each output occurrence consumes one available occurrence from the first array.
Edge cases: Duplicates are preserved up to the smaller frequency; empty inputs yield an empty list.
complexity_reason: The first array is counted once and the second is scanned once.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
notes:
Task: Return the multiset intersection of two arrays.
Idea: Count the first array in a map and decrement a count when a matching value is appended from the second.
Invariant: Map counts represent unused occurrences from the first array.
Edge cases: An occurrence is appended only while its count is positive, so duplicates are bounded by both inputs.
complexity_reason: The map stores counts for the first array and each input is scanned once.
